title: Design Ticket Booking
subtitle: Watch 200,000 fans fight for 20,000 seats, and see how holds, expiry and a waiting room prevent double booking.
learn: Why seat inventory is a contention problem, not a throughput problem
How a temporary hold with an expiry claims a seat atomically
Why the database, not the app server, must be the final judge of who owns a seat
How a virtual waiting room turns a stampede into a steady trickle
How payment, hold expiry and confirmation fit into one seat state machine

steps.title: 20,000 seats, 200,000 fans
steps.body: Tickets for a stadium show go on sale at 10:00. The venue has 20,000 seats and about 200,000 fans arrive in the first minute. Most traffic is not buying, it is refreshing and picking seats. The hard part is not speed alone: two people must never end up owning the same seat, and a seat in someone's cart should not be lost forever if they walk away.
steps.idea: Ticketing is a contention problem: many users, a small fixed inventory, and zero tolerance for double sales.
steps.caption: A huge crowd aims at a small, fixed inventory.

steps.title: The naive version breaks
steps.body: A simple design reads the seat, checks it is free, then writes the sale. Two requests can both read 'free' before either writes, so both succeed. That is a race condition: the check and the write are separate steps. With thousands of people clicking seat A12 at once, double sales are guaranteed, and no amount of extra servers fixes it.
steps.idea: Check-then-write is unsafe; the check and the claim must be one atomic operation.
steps.caption: Two requests both see A12 as free.

steps.title: Claim the seat atomically
steps.body: Let the database arbitrate. A conditional update such as 'set owner = me WHERE seat = A12 AND status = available' succeeds for exactly one caller, because the database serialises writes to the same row. The loser gets zero rows changed and is told to pick another seat. Optimistic version checks or a unique constraint on (event, seat) give the same guarantee.
steps.idea: Let a single authority with an atomic conditional write decide; losers just retry elsewhere.
steps.caption: One conditional UPDATE wins; the rest get zero rows.

steps.title: Holds with an expiry
steps.body: Buying takes minutes: choose seats, enter card details, maybe 3DS. So a click moves the seat from available to held, owned by that user until a deadline, typically 5 to 10 minutes. The hold lives in a fast store such as Redis with a TTL (time to live), set only if the key does not exist, so a hold can be claimed once and disappears on its own. The database still records the final sale.
steps.idea: A hold is a lease: it reserves the seat now and releases itself if the buyer goes quiet.
steps.caption: Seat A12 is held for 8 minutes.

steps.title: Pay, then confirm
steps.body: The user pays while the hold is ticking. The API calls the payment provider with an idempotency key so a retry cannot charge twice (payments have their own lesson). On success, one database transaction checks the hold is still theirs and flips the seat to sold. The order matters: never confirm a seat the buyer has not paid for, and never charge for a seat that was lost.
steps.idea: Seat state changes to sold only inside a transaction that re-checks hold ownership after payment succeeds.
steps.caption: Payment succeeds, seat becomes sold.

steps.title: The buyer walks away
steps.body: Most holds are abandoned: people close the tab or change their mind. When the TTL passes, the hold key vanishes and the seat becomes buyable again without any code running. A sweeper job also reconciles the database, resetting seats whose hold deadline has passed, as a backstop if the hold store restarted. A late payment on an expired hold must be refunded or re-checked, never silently double sold.
steps.idea: Expiry returns abandoned inventory to the pool, and the database remains the source of truth.
steps.caption: Expired holds release seats back to sale.

steps.title: The stampede problem
steps.body: Atomic claims keep data correct but not the system healthy. If 200,000 users hammer the seat map, the database melts and everyone gets errors, including people who would have succeeded. Seat maps are read-heavy, so serve them from a cache with a second or two of staleness, and accept that a clicked seat may turn out taken. The claim, not the display, enforces correctness.
steps.idea: Protect the write path: cache reads loosely, and let only the claim be strict.
steps.caption: Too many shoppers overload the claim path.

steps.title: Virtual waiting room
steps.body: Put a queue in front. Arrivals get a random position (random, so refreshing early earns nothing) and wait on a lightweight page served from a CDN. The room admits a fixed number, say 2,000 shoppers, and lets in more as others finish or time out. Admitted users carry a signed token the API checks. The database now sees thousands of users, not hundreds of thousands.
steps.idea: A waiting room converts a spike into a steady, admission-controlled flow the backend can handle.
steps.caption: Only 2,000 shoppers are admitted at a time.

steps.title: Fairness and sellouts
steps.body: Random order is fairer than first-come-first-served, which rewards fast connections and bots. Limit tickets per account (say 4) and require login or verification before admission to slow scalpers. If an event sells out in minutes, the room can show 'sold out' to everyone still waiting instead of making them queue for nothing. The cost is complexity: another system that must itself never fall over.
steps.idea: Admission control is a product decision as well as an engineering one: fairness, anti-bot, and honesty.
steps.caption: Admitted shoppers hold and buy; the rest wait.

steps.title: Safe under pressure
steps.body: Throttle the crowd with a waiting room, hold seats with expiring leases, take payment, and let the database's atomic write decide the final owner. The cache and hold store absorb pressure; the database guarantees no seat is sold twice. Each seat moves through available, held, sold, and back to available when a hold expires.
steps.idea: Correctness lives in one atomic claim; everything else exists to keep that claim fast and fair.
steps.caption: Every seat has exactly one owner at a time.

quiz.q: Two buyers click seat A12 in the same millisecond. Which design reliably prevents a double sale?
options: Check the seat is free in app code, then write the sale
Use more app servers so each request is faster
A conditional database write that only succeeds if the seat is still available
Show a warning in the UI when someone else is looking at the seat
quiz.why: Only an atomic claim by one authority guarantees a single winner. Check-then-write has a race window, faster servers just shrink it, and UI warnings are advisory.

quiz.q: Why give a seat hold a TTL instead of waiting for the user to cancel?
options: TTLs make payments faster
Abandoned carts are common, and expiry returns those seats to sale automatically
It removes the need for a database
It lets two users hold the same seat
quiz.why: Many users never finish. A TTL makes the hold a lease that frees itself, so inventory is not stranded by people who left.

quiz.q: The seat map is cached for 2 seconds and shows A12 free, but it was just taken. What happens when a user clicks it?
options: They buy it twice
The atomic claim fails and they are asked to pick another seat
The cache is corrupted and must be flushed
The hold store grants it anyway
quiz.why: Displays may be stale, but correctness is enforced at claim time, so the loser simply gets a 'taken' response.

quiz.q: What is the main reason to add a virtual waiting room?
options: To make the atomic update unnecessary
To limit concurrent shoppers so the booking path stays healthy
To make payments cheaper
To sort buyers by internet speed
quiz.why: The waiting room admits a controlled number of users. It protects capacity and does not replace atomic claims.

quiz.q: A payment succeeds at 8 minutes 5 seconds, but the hold expired at 8 minutes and another user holds the seat. What should the system do?
options: Give the seat to both users
Confirm anyway and ignore the other hold
Fail the confirmation and refund, because the hold is no longer theirs
Delete the other user's hold silently
quiz.why: Confirmation must re-check ownership inside the transaction. If the lease is lost, refund rather than breaking the one-owner rule.

cheatsheet.def: A single conditional write (UPDATE ... WHERE status = available) that only one concurrent caller can win.
A temporary reservation with a deadline, typically 5 to 10 minutes, that frees itself if unused.
Redis command: set a key only if absent, with an expiry. Gives a one-winner hold that auto-releases.
available -> held -> sold, with held -> available on expiry or cancel. Only legal transitions are allowed.
Admission-controlled queue that lets in a fixed number of shoppers; often randomised for fairness.
The database records final ownership. Caches and hold stores are fast helpers, never the last word.
A unique ID on the payment call so retries never charge twice.

lab.prompt: Design ticket sales for a 50,000-seat stadium where 500,000 people show up at on-sale time. Describe the seat model, how holds work, how double booking is prevented, how the waiting room protects the backend, and how failures like abandoned carts and late payments are handled.
requirements: Define seat states and the allowed transitions between them
Choose a hold duration and explain how expiry releases seats
Show the exact write that makes a claim atomic
Describe how the waiting room admits users and what token the API checks
Estimate peak requests per second to the booking path with and without the room
Explain what happens if payment succeeds after the hold expired
Say how the seat map stays fast despite heavy reads
hints: If 500,000 users each make 1 request per second, that is 500,000 requests per second; the room might cap shoppers at 5,000
A unique constraint on (event_id, seat_id) can enforce one owner even if app code has a bug
Ask what is lost if the hold store restarts and forgets all holds
Seat maps can be a cached snapshot refreshed every second or two
Think about per-account ticket limits and bots when picking admission order
checklist: Seat states and transitions are explicit
Claim is atomic and enforced by the database
Holds expire without relying on the user
Backend load is capped by admission control
Late payment on an expired hold is handled with a refund or re-check
Stale seat map views cannot cause double booking
